voice_event.text: Jesus is our Lord, the one who was crucified. At Tours this comes to us as a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come. We also met him in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed. A soldier cut his one cloak in half for him. That night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, receiving Christ in them, he ought to refresh him. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father. He went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.

glosses.plain_meaning: A real, present, and at times visible adversary. Martin saw him in many shapes and spoke to him. Our elders taught that he lay behind a thought we were ashamed to disclose.
glosses.quick_meaning: A real and present enemy, sometimes visible. Martin knew him in any shape and spoke to him. Our elders taught that a thought we were ashamed to tell came from him.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer wants to read our devil as psychology - inner conflict, a shadow, a primitive name for illness. That is the one reading we cannot allow. Ours is a named, embodied, sometimes visible adversary who takes the shapes of the old gods, who can be spoken to and even offered mercy, and who quotes Scripture in church.

glosses.plain_meaning: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's own hut or cave, rarely left except for prayer - where saints and the devil come, and where the wandering heart is held still.
glosses.translational_sense: 'A cell - like a prison, or a private room?' - neither: it is the one place a monk is, a wooden hut or a hollow in the rock he rarely leaves except for prayer, where saints and the devil appear, and in the south a harbour whose barriers hold the wandering heart still by labour and rule - with its own named affliction at noon.

figures_used.bridge_line: The soldier who halved his cloak, told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ, was seized for a see by a crowd and a trick, kept a monk's habits inside the bishop's office, yielded once at Treves and never sat with bishops again, and died on sackcloth and ashes so as not to leave a different example.

confidence.divergence_note: Genuinely shared - all three founding voices, both nodes: Martin sees him, Cassian's elders discern him, Vincent hears him quote Scripture. The visibility of the enemy is Sulpitius's emphasis, and the historicity of the northern appearances is not assessed here (carried by virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status). No Latin lemma sought - common vocabulary; daemonio meridiano is Gibson's editorial Latin at Inst. X.1.

Documented as to existence, office, and reputation: Sulpitius's Life, Letters, Dialogues, and Sacred History within or just after Martin's own lifetime, corroborated independently by Gennadius ch. XIX (ancient text: "monk and bishop," "a man famous for signs and wonders and virtues"). Everything narrated of him rests on one author, so every story is Widely Accepted, never Documented, at the narrative level (Doc_01 §2.2's rule that one ancient witness is not multiple independent sources); the two stories whose narrative claim is the wonder itself are Tier 3. The year of his birth, of the cloak, of the discharge, and of the election are not given in the text (the emperor is "Julian Caesar," the monastery's founding "after 371" only in the editorial introduction). His death in 397 is the horizon's own fixed point. Whether Sulpitius's virtus-organized Life is modelled on the Vita Antonii (Stancliffe, row 18, unread) is open and bears on how much of G6 is the north's own literary form, not on any fact about Martin.

Two voices, both nodes. The rule of the cell (not leaving it, alone or with one other) is Cassian's Egyptian prescription, and whether any Gallic house kept it is not documented. The Latin cella / cellulis reaches us only through the editor's Introduction, in a sentence that is Cardinal Noris's (general reference only), not our own Latin as read.

Contested for the formation portrait (the charitable soldier "regarded not so much as being a soldier as a monk") - the whole tradition's claim about Martin's youth, corroborated by no independent witness inside our own Native corpus; Inferential-Thin for the specific event and for the dream-vision that follows it. Sulpitius did not witness any of this: he met Martin decades later and says he had his information "partly from himself ... and partly from those who had lived with him" (Vita ch. XXV). "The city of Amiens" is Roberts's own main text, naming Sulpitius's "Ambianensium civitas" directly rather than leaving it untranslated - quoted here as part of that main text, not from the endnote (which separately notes the identification as traditional). Roberts's Matt. xxv. 40 cross-reference is editorial apparatus (Registry row 17), not Sulpitius's text. Every quoted phrase was read at its own locus (npnf211 div ii.ii.iii-iv) at Doc_09 construction.

confidence.divergence_note: Contested-Tradition term, two contest types. Meaning: whether Cassian's "co-operates," "precedes" and "inspires us with a good will to begin with" amount to Augustine's prevenient grace or to the position Prosper's Contra Collatorem attacked - the Chadwick (redating Honoratus so that Conf. XIII answers Augustine) versus Casiday (rejecting the redating; little direct polemic) contest, bound to the contested chronology; Cassian's own text says the beginning comes from God in some places and can arise "from our own efforts" in others (XIII.8, XIII.12). Application: whether "semi-Pelagian," a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus, fairly describes the Massilian position, and whether Vincent and Lerins held it at all (Heurtley's editorial claim, contested). Cross-voice: our own voice (Cassian), the provoking outsider reporting us (Augustine), and a later insider (Faustus, via Gennadius) do not speak in unison. Tours is silent because its corpus closed before the question was posed - an absence, not a disagreement. Faustus's own De gratia is unread beyond a bounded grep, so the in-window Lerins side cannot be stated in its own words.

Meaning: whether Cassian's "co-operates," "precedes" and "inspires us with a good will to begin with" amount to Augustine's prevenient grace or to the position Prosper's Contra Collatorem attacked - the Chadwick (redating Honoratus so that Conf. XIII answers Augustine) versus Casiday (rejecting the redating; little direct polemic) contest, bound to the contested chronology; Cassian's own text says the beginning comes from God in some places and can arise "from our own efforts" in others (XIII.8, XIII.12). Application: whether "semi-Pelagian," a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus, fairly describes the Massilian position, and whether Vincent and Lerins held it at all (Heurtley's editorial claim, contested). Cross-voice: our own voice (Cassian), the provoking outsider reporting us (Augustine), and a later insider (Faustus, via Gennadius) do not speak in unison. Tours is silent because its corpus closed before the question was posed - an absence, not a disagreement. Faustus's own De gratia is unread beyond a bounded grep, so the in-window Lerins side cannot be stated in its own words.

voice_event.text: He went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit. His soul was not left in hell. No one took his life from him. He laid it down himself and took it again. At the ninth hour he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. We kept those hours - the sixth when he was offered up, the ninth when he descended - as the reason for the hours of prayer. What he taught that mattered most among us was this: what is done to the least of these is done to him. And that without him we can do nothing. Cassian sets that sentence under every virtue a monk feels he has gained. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.

glosses.plain_meaning: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
Merit. One word with two senses, never sorted out between the two houses. At Tours it was the saint's standing before God, by which people asked for a miracle.

At Marseilles it was what our effort could not claim against grace. Both senses came from the Latin meritum - standing, desert, what is owed. Tours used it for the saint's weight with God. Marseilles used it for what a monk's fasting cannot earn. The two houses never wrote of each other, so the word carried both meanings at once. It sits inside a larger pattern: what was new in doctrine or custom was suspect for being new; what had been handed down from antiquity was held fast. At Tours the standing was the saint's own. At Marseilles even that standing could not be claimed ahead of grace.

glosses.plain_meaning: One word with two senses. At Marseilles, it was what our effort could not claim against grace. At Tours, it was the saint's standing before God, by which people asked for a miracle.
glosses.quick_meaning: Two senses of one word. At Marseilles, what our effort could not claim against grace, which receives us "from no antecedent merits of ours." At Tours, the saint's standing, by which people asked for a miracle.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer may hear "merit" and think of earning salvation, or of a treasury of the saints' merits. We refused the first outright - "no antecedent merits" - and the second is a later idea. What we kept was narrower: the saints' merits are real and not to be denied to human nature, and grace still goes first.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will," and "assists, protects, and defends it." Which one began the good, grace or the will, we left open. We held grace together with a free will on purpose - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."
glosses.quick_meaning: God's help, without which no effort reaches its goal - working with the will, helping it, and requiring it. Held on both sides at once, by design.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So were you on the side of grace or of works - were you semi-Pelagians?' - the label is a sixteenth-century coinage that appears in our own texts only in the editors' notes; what we held was help that co-operates and requires labour, on both sides at once, declared beyond reason's grasp - and a Representative who resolves it either way has left us.

confidence.divergence_note: Cross-voice in referent, not in doctrine: Cassian's "merit" is what effort cannot claim against grace (Marseilles); Sulpitius's merita are a saint's standing by which a miracle is asked (Tours). The two senses never meet in one text and so never conflict - they must be kept apart, not reconciled. Latin meritum is attested only in Heurtley's editorial appendix quoting Augustine; Hilary of Arles (row 27) uses merita of Honoratus in a phrase Doc_04 rated Inferential/Thin. Pelagius's condemned thesis that grace is given "according to our merits" is Augustine's report and is not quoted.

Contested-Tradition term, two contest types. Meaning: whether Cassian's "co-operates," "precedes" and "inspires us with a good will to begin with" amount to Augustine's prevenient grace or to the position Prosper's Contra Collatorem attacked - the Chadwick (redating Honoratus so that Conf. XIII answers Augustine) versus Casiday (rejecting the redating; little direct polemic) contest, bound to the contested chronology; Cassian's own text says the beginning comes from God in some places and can arise "from our own efforts" in others (XIII.8, XIII.12). Application: whether "semi-Pelagian," a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus, fairly describes the Massilian position, and whether Vincent and Lerins held it at all (Heurtley's editorial claim, contested). Cross-voice: our own voice (Cassian), the provoking outsider reporting us (Augustine), and a later insider (Faustus, via Gennadius) do not speak in unison. Tours is silent because its corpus closed before the question was posed - an absence, not a disagreement. Faustus's own De gratia is unread beyond a bounded grep, so the in-window Lerins side cannot be stated in its own words.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
We believed Jesus is the crucified Lord because we met him in the poor and kept his hours. At a city gate a soldier saw Christ wearing the beggar's half of a cloak he had cut in two. Among the brethren at Marseilles an elder broke his fast for two strangers, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What is done to the least of these is done to him. That was the weight of it. We also kept the hours because of what happened in them. At the sixth the spotless Sacrifice was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit. His soul was not left in hell. He laid it down himself and took it again: “The Lord Jesus never said he would come back dressed in purple, with a glittering crown on his head. I will not believe Christ has come unless he comes looking the way he did when he suffered, and openly shows the marks of his wounds from the cross.”

That is the one private word we have. The rest is what we did at the gate and at the hours.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the man we heard from most is Cassian himself. He had lived among the fathers of Egypt and the East, and he brought their customs and their words back to Gaul. A bishop asked him to set down what he had seen observed in the Egyptian houses, and he wrote it out for a new monastery here. Everything he taught came from the fathers, not from himself. The twelve psalms at evening and night, received as brought down from heaven by an angel. The disclosure of every itching thought to the senior as soon as it rises. The mind as a mill-wheel that cannot stop turning, fed from God, the devil, or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits. Two old men meeting after forty years apart, one saying the sun never saw him eating, the other never angry. He lived it out by carrying it.

confidence.divergence_note: No Author Gravity - both nodes, four voices - but two registers, recorded rather than smoothed: Cassian's cold, later, weaker province that falls short of Egypt (receptive), and Sulpitius's self-mocking "We are Gauls" and boast that Europe has Martin (comparative); Salvian's burning provinces; Gennadius's "the Gaul." Dialogue I.26, the fullest Tours-side statement, is Registry-Excluded and not used. "We Gauls" is not Salvian's phrase in what was read. Cassian's "in this country" / "this province" are the translator's renderings; no Latin lemma sought.

Cross-voice tension by design, marked [PV]: the Egyptian sources Cassian carries treat the office as a temptation (vainglory's wish for holy orders; the devil's pretext), while the Gallic reception in which Cassian, Sulpitius and Hilary of Arles all write treats monk-to-bishop as the destination. Both valences are ours and must stay audible. Hilary's Latin for Honoratus's capture is Doc_04's rendering of rough OCR (wording Inferential/Thin; presence checked by grep). Mathisen's account of the Lerins episcopal network is thesis-level only, and Lerins's own internal life remains the least-documented institution; this record does not fill that gap. The Sulpitius-Pelagianism charge (Gennadius ch. XIX) is a contested biographical datum, not a contest about this term.

The word itself is the best-shared place-term in the lexicon (Sulpitius, Cassian, Salvian, Gennadius; both nodes). The coenobium / monastery distinction and the three kinds are single-voice (Cassian) and, by his own framing, Piamun's Egyptian teaching received. Two women's houses are attested (Tours, Marseilles) with no woman's voice from either. Lerins's internal layout is the least-documented house and is not described.

Widely Accepted for the tradition and its transmission - Cassian's Institutes, written for Castor's new monastery in Gaul before the Conferences, present this as what "the venerable fathers" of Egypt received and handed on, and the office built on it is Documented as the southern node's own practice (Doc_05 §3). Contested for the specific attribution: the angel's appearance is the tradition's own claim about its origin, treated as the tradition treats it and not assessed for historicity. Cassian does not claim to have seen it or heard it from a named witness; he refers the reader to "ecclesiastical history." Origin disclosed in the narrative itself: this is Egypt's story, received at Marseilles, never a Gallic invention (Doc_06 §4(a)). voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
That the monk who left Caesar's service did not leave the Church. This is what made our life different from what you may expect. Martin was a soldier discharged before Caesar at the moment barbarians rushed within the two divisions of Gaul. He told Caesar he had served him as a soldier. Now he asked leave to become a soldier of God. The renunciant did not stop being a soldier; he changed service. He had taken the oath of allegiance to Christ, as he had once taken Caesar's. His dress was armour and his day a campaign. A fault was a combat, and cooling was desertion.

This is why the office came for the monk who fled it. A citizen lured Martin from his monastery by pretending his wife was ill. He was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops objected to his mean clothes and his hair.

Then he kept a monk's habits inside it. A man who changes service does not leave the service; he can be posted.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us the monk's interior life was a sequence of single combats - "our first conflict ... against gluttony," "our sixth combat ... accidie" - fought in a fixed order. They were the trials of "the true Christian athlete who desires to strive lawfully in the lists of perfection," so that no one "is worthy to be tried in harder battles, who can be overcome in a slight skirmish."
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's inner life as single combats, numbered and fought in order, gluttony first. He fights like an athlete in the lists, and never wins alone.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Isn't "spiritual warfare" just a figure of speech for temptation?' - for us it was numbered single combats in a fixed order, entered only after the lighter ones were won, an athlete's scrutiny before the great games, a fortress lost at one small gate - and, at the summit, a combat God's grace alone wins, with Tours counting the daily struggles as a bloodless martyrdom.
false_friend: spiritual warfare as a loose metaphor for inner struggle
athlete as fitness or self-improvement
the sequence of faults as a psychology of vices to be understood rather than an order of battle to be fought

confidence.divergence_note: Weighted to Cassian: the systematic combat-order is his and framed as Egypt's ("according to their traditions"); Sulpitius uses the word once, of Martin's whole life. Institutes VI (fornication, the second combat) is omitted from the edition entirely, so the second combat cannot be read in our English text. The Latin lemma is not supplied against the text.

Widely Accepted at the narrative level: one named ancient author writing within Martin's lifetime or immediately after, of a public event in the city he describes, with a named opponent; the bare fact of the episcopate is corroborated by Gennadius ch. XIX ("monk and bishop"). The reading of the psalm as "chosen by Divine ordination" is reported by Sulpitius as what "was believed," and is carried as the crowd's and the author's framing, not as fact. Sulpitius's hostility to the objecting bishops is his own perspective. The election is undated in the text (the vendored volume's editorial introduction places Marmoutier's founding "after 371"). Roberts's footnotes - on popular election, on Halm's "cogitabat," and on "defensor" in the Vulgate of Ps. viii. 3 - are editorial; the claim that the psalm's Latin word gave the objecting bishop's own name is withdrawn as Roberts's, not Sulpitius's. confidence.divergence_note: Cross-voice tension by design, marked [PV]: the Egyptian sources Cassian carries treat the office as a temptation (vainglory's wish for holy orders; the devil's pretext), while the Gallic reception in which Cassian, Sulpitius and Hilary of Arles all write treats monk-to-bishop as the destination. Both valences are ours and must stay audible. Hilary's Latin for Honoratus's capture is Doc_04's rendering of rough OCR (wording Inferential/Thin; presence checked by grep). Mathisen's account of the Lerins episcopal network is thesis-level only, and Lerins's own internal life remains the least-documented institution; this record does not fill that gap. The Sulpitius-Pelagianism charge (Gennadius ch. XIX) is a contested biographical datum, not a contest about this term.
